entry.title: Columbia launches a Don’t Panic Room in latest campaign
entry.summary: Creative Inspiration Columbia launches a Don’t Panic Room in latest campaign Created by adam&eveTBWA, the work takes aim at tech billionaires’ apocalyptic tendencies while offering outdoor enthusiasts the chance to win a fully stocked bunker By Rebecca Fulleylove 29/10/2026 3:53
entry.content:
Creative Inspiration

Columbia launches a Don’t Panic Room in latest campaign

Created by adam&eveTBWA, the work takes aim at tech billionaires’ apocalyptic tendencies while offering outdoor enthusiasts the chance to win a fully stocked bunker

By Rebecca Fulleylove 29/10/2026 3:53 am

In recent years, Columbia Sportswear has become known for its tongue-in-cheek approach to outdoor advertising, often putting its gear to the test in deliberately absurd scenarios.

Its latest campaign, created by adam&eve\TBWA, centres around the Don’t Panic Room – a campaign and contest inviting audiences to showcase their survival skills for the chance to win a fully stocked, off-grid bunker equipped with Columbia gear and survival essentials.

Directed by Benji Weinstein and produced by Smuggler, the film takes aim at the “wealthy tech bros” preparing for the apocalypse in private bunkers, arguing that ordinary outdoor enthusiasts deserve a shot at survival, too.

Fronting the film is Columbia CEO Tim Boyle, whose appearances in previous campaigns, including last year’s open letter to Flat Earthers, have helped establish his place in the brand’s irreverent advertising. This time, he invites viewers to prove their survival skills, with the campaign imagining how Columbia’s gear could come in handy when the world takes a turn for the worse.

The campaign’s more playful touches include puffer jackets sealed in cans, dubbed “canned heat”, ready to be opened in an emergency. Featuring Columbia’s Omni-Heat Infinity thermal-reflective technology, the jackets bring a product-focused twist to the survivalist concept.

Of course the apparel is only part of the prize, the main draw is the 40ft-by-8ft modified shipping container that comes equipped with a kitchen, bathroom, bunk bed and survival supplies, as well as a robotic dog named Rocky.

“The Don’t Panic Room is the perfect embodiment of Columbia’s brand platform, Engineered For Whatever, celebrating the ingenuity, irreverence and spirit of adventure that define the brand,” says Ant Nelson, chief creative officer at adam&eve\TBWA.

The campaign launched on social media, alongside a print ad in the New York Times and billboards across Silicon Valley, poking fun at the tech elite’s obsession with preparing for disaster. Entries are open until the end of November, with participants able to submit videos showcasing their outdoor survival skills via Instagram or Columbia’s website.

entry.title: The Monthly Interview: Kirsten Rutherford
entry.summary: Creative Insight The Monthly Interview: Kirsten Rutherford DoorDash’s ECD reflects on leaving the agency world behind, the art of building strong partnerships, and how everyday human truths drive the brand’s most creative work By Rebecca Fulleylove 29/10/2026 3:30 am Kirsten Ruth
entry.content:
Creative Insight

The Monthly Interview: Kirsten Rutherford

DoorDash’s ECD reflects on leaving the agency world behind, the art of building strong partnerships, and how everyday human truths drive the brand’s most creative work

By Rebecca Fulleylove 29/10/2026 3:30 am

Kirsten Rutherford’s first experience of advertising involved a sugar rush and a room full of rainbow markers. Her father was managing director of Leo Burnett Auckland, and while he worked weekends, she would run wild through the creatives’ offices, drawing with their marker pens and leaving the lids off, all the while drinking Sprite (one of the agency’s clients). “Those poor art directors would come in on Monday to discover their very expensive tools had dried out,” she tells CR. “But I remember being incredibly happy there.”

By the age of eight, Rutherford had already decided she wanted to be a copywriter. Decades later, after a career spanning New Zealand, London and the US, and agencies including TBWA\Chiat\Day, Team One, 72andSunny and Wieden+Kennedy, she has taken her curiosity about creativity to the other side of the business. At the beginning of 2026, she joined DoorDash as executive creative director, leading its in-house creative studio, Superette.

The move was driven by a desire to get closer to the problems behind the advertising. “I’d had offers from brands before, but DoorDash was the first that shared my creative ambition,” she says. “It’s a business full of fascinating problems, with a seriously talented creative crew. It was an easy yes.” For the creative, being inside the business means spotting opportunities before they become briefs and seeing how creativity can answer real business problems.

Top: In Case of Emergency campaign; Above: Order, Delivered campaign; © DoorDash

At 17, while finishing high school, Rutherford responded to a creative brief in a national newspaper for the Axis Idea School, a night course run by New Zealand’s leading agencies. She was one of 12 people selected, and much younger than most of her classmates. “There were university graduates and people coming from all sorts of different careers and walks of life,” she says. “One of the best creatives I know came through the course having been a sheep farmer, which is very Kiwi.”

The course gave her the beginnings of a portfolio and led to an internship at DDB. She was studying marketing at university when M&C Saatchi offered her a copywriting job after her first semester. She took it, and never completed her degree. “So I still don’t have a degree, but I’ve managed to find my way creatively around the world.”

Much of Rutherford’s career has been shaped by the places she’s lived in, and moving between countries taught her to question her assumptions. “What’s funny, what’s obvious, what people care about – you have to learn all of that again. It teaches you to listen,” she says.

New Zealand gave her resourcefulness and “a healthy lack of preciousness”; London sharpened her appreciation for craft, while America expanded her sense of what was possible. Her experiences across different agencies also helped shape her approach to leadership. “People do their best work when they feel equally challenged and supported,” she says. “When they can feel safe enough to share something unhinged or unfinished and trust that everyone wants to make it better.”

DoorDash has a lovely connection to real life: what people need, what they crave, what they’ve forgotten, what might make their day a little better

At DoorDash, Superette’s remit spans creative work for Consumer, Dasher and Merchant audiences, stewardship of the brand’s voice and design, and partnerships supporting its Ads Platform, co-marketing, and growth partners. Working closely with teams across strategy, social, operations, marketing, growth and insights gives the studio a close understanding of the business and the people it serves.

A recent example is Order, Delivered, a campaign that finds creative possibility in everyday chaos. Using a DoorDash delivery photo as a starting point, the films reveal the stories behind the orders, from new parents whose plans are derailed by a nappy emergency to a sleep-deprived mother ordering postpartum essentials like formula, nipple cream, ice cream and a robot vacuum.

The situations are specific but relatable. “Our Order, Delivered work shows how much creative possibility there is in paying attention to those everyday truths,” Rutherford says. “DoorDash has a lovely connection to real life: what people need, what they crave, what they’ve forgotten, what might make their day a little better. There’s an enormous amount of human behaviour to be curious about.”

The In Case Of campaign, developed in partnership with Gut, takes that thinking in a different direction. Reimagining the familiar emergency box, it explores DoorDash’s ability to deliver almost anything in almost any situation, from bandages for runners experiencing chafing during a marathon to baseball gloves in case of foul balls at Wrigley Field.

“The fun comes from where those boxes show up, what’s inside and why you might need it,” Rutherford says. “The connection between the situation and the object makes the idea work.”

The brand’s wider collaborations this year span equally varied territory. With MikeTeeVee, Superette developed Don’t Fan for Free, a football campaign featuring Bill Belichick as the brand’s Fan Coach, and It’s All in the Delivery, starring New York Knicks player Josh Hart.

Our internal team has a closeness to the business that brings depth. Our agency partners have a little distance, which allows them to bring equal passion, but a different perspective

Other projects – while not led by Superette – similarly round out the picture of the brand’s creative landscape. Loop, for instance, recently helped create CringeMart, a humorous in-app storefront for life’s most awkward purchases, supported by hidden-camera films and live condom-counter billboards. Wieden+Kennedy Toronto’s Not That Dramatic took a cinematic approach to the everyday dilemma of ordering dinner.

For Rutherford, knowing when to bring in external partners is part of balancing creative ambition with commercial demands. “Our internal team has a closeness to the business that brings depth. Our agency partners have a little distance, which allows them to bring equal passion, but a different perspective.”

The decision depends on the problem, the expertise required and where a partner could strengthen the work. What matters is establishing clear responsibilities and a relationship in which people can challenge one another without becoming territorial. “I want our partners to feel close enough to the business to understand it, and trusted enough to challenge us.”

Rutherford’s belief in collaboration extends far beyond daily agency operations – it has also opened doors for creativity to make a broader social impact. Sometimes those opportunities stem directly from long-standing relationships.

After working with CMO Janell Holas on a detergent brand, Rutherford stayed in touch long after the account ended. When Holas later took the helm as CMO of Make-A-Wish, that connection allowed Rutherford to lend her creative support to the organisation’s mission on several occasions.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Josh Hart 🏀 (@jhart)

Other times, the connection is deeply personal. While at TBWA\Chiat\Day, she leapt at the chance to work on Gatorade’s Sisters in Sweat, a campaign encouraging young girls to stay involved in sports. Having taught group exercise for years, the topic hit close to home.

“I know first-hand what movement can give you, so I really wanted to be involved,” she says. “I wrote a letter for Serena Williams to read to her newborn daughter, and it was a joy to see Sisters in Sweat come to life.”

Exploring what girls gain from sport – and what they stand to lose when they drop out – exemplifies for Rutherford how creativity can spotlight experiences that deserve recognition. It also served as a reminder of how easily leaders can mistake their own background for a universal truth.

“Your own experience is just one perspective,” she notes. “The people around the table will see things you don’t, if you simply give them the room to contribute.” She wants to see greater transparency around progression in the creative industries, broader routes into creative roles and more active sponsorship of people whose work deserves to be seen. “Representation needs to come with influence and opportunity. Leaders need to look honestly at who is getting both, and take responsibility for changing that.”

Having entered advertising through the Axis Idea School, Rutherford understands the importance of opening doors. She believes that emerging talent needs useful feedback, meaningful opportunities and the confidence to develop their own voice. “We can be rigorous about an idea while helping someone understand that feedback on the work isn’t a verdict on their talent or their future,” she says.

Her advice to creatives progressing into leadership is to stay curious about the work and the people around it, without losing enthusiasm for the craft. “Look at things, talk about ideas, care about the details. Be a ridiculously overexcited ad nerd,” she says.

“Don’t be afraid to share your enthusiasm for whatever weird subculture brings you joy (even if that means rave music, old rescue dogs, drag and cake). Enthusiasm is infectious, and it matters even more when you’re leading.”

As Rutherford sees it, leadership is about learning to take satisfaction in helping others make something brilliant. It means creating the conditions for people to do their best work and leaving room for them to surprise you. For someone whose earliest memories of an agency involved being given the freedom to draw all over the place, it feels like a fitting philosophy.

entry.title: Oxford Street gets its first ever brand identity as it enters a new era
entry.summary: Creative Inspiration Oxford Street gets its first ever brand identity as it enters a new era The work by Koto accompanies the pedestrianisation of the capital’s busiest shopping street, a destination long associated with congestion and retail decline By Adam Woodward 29/10/2026 3
entry.content:
Creative Inspiration

Oxford Street gets its first ever brand identity as it enters a new era

The work by Koto accompanies the pedestrianisation of the capital’s busiest shopping street, a destination long associated with congestion and retail decline

By Adam Woodward 29/10/2026 3:18 am

Oxford Street has a new brand identity, created by Koto to accompany the pedestrianisation of a stretch of the central London thoroughfare. Titled For Everyone, the identity is intended to help reposition one of Britain’s most recognisable – and much-maligned – streets as a destination for culture, leisure and public life, as well as retail.

Developed in partnership with the Greater London Authority (GLA) and the Oxford Street Development Corporation (OSDC), the branding coincides with the recent transformation of the section between Orchard Street and Great Portland Street into a traffic-free space.

The project arrives at a pivotal moment for Oxford Street, which has spent years wrestling the challenges facing high streets up and down the country. Once a symbol of London’s commercial vitality, it has become synonymous for many with overcrowded pavements, pollution and an increasingly frustrating visitor experience, alongside concerns about the steady decline of bricks-and-mortar retail.

Pedestrianisation offers an opportunity to rethink what the street is for, rather than simply how people move through it. According to the OSDC, removing traffic creates more scope for walking, gathering and public events, while giving the surrounding businesses a setting better suited to spending time in rather than merely passing through.

The challenge for Koto was to translate that new proposition into a compelling brand. As Koto founder and CEO James Greenfield noted, “Oxford Street’s purpose is set in the minds of most. We set out to build an identity around what has always made it extraordinary: its ability to constantly change, set against the broader question of retail in the 21st century.”

At the heart of the identity is a wordmark that places emphasis on the word ‘for’, framing Oxford Street as a destination with multiple purposes and audiences. The idea is backed up by the slogan ‘Where London meets’: for shopping and stopping, walking and talking, and for the millions of people who live and work in the city.

The visual system pairs London Sans and London Serif typefaces, bringing together the capital’s contemporary character and the street’s history. A green palette signals the ambition for a greener public realm, with more room for pedestrians to move, meet and pause, while secondary colourways appear across wayfinding and supporting messaging.

Sam Howard, creative director at Koto, says the intention was to capture the vast array of experiences that make the street so distinctive. “Oxford Street brings together so much of what makes London extraordinary. It’s a place of firsts, of celebration, of everyday encounters. We wanted to capture that wild, wonderful energy in a brand that feels true to its history and optimistic about its future.”

Whether the new identity can help restore Oxford Street’s appeal will depend on more than branding alone. The quality of the public space, the mix of businesses and the experiences available will ultimately determine whether it becomes somewhere people choose to spend time, rather than simply endure on their way elsewhere.

But with pedestrianisation beginning to reshape its character, the project gives Oxford Street a new story to tell – and a chance to announce its traffic-free future in style.

entry.title: On living and working with anxiety
entry.summary: Creative Insight On living and working with anxiety Beast Film’s Victoria Taylor shares her experiences with the “uninvited guest” of anxiety and how she’s turned them into a short film By Victoria Taylor 28/10/2026 3:45 am I felt inspired recently by the likes of Caitlin Moran a
entry.content:
Creative Insight

On living and working with anxiety

Beast Film’s Victoria Taylor shares her experiences with the “uninvited guest” of anxiety and how she’s turned them into a short film

By Victoria Taylor 28/10/2026 3:45 am

I felt inspired recently by the likes of Caitlin Moran and Anita Rani, who have spoken publicly about their anxiety. Bold, confident, hugely talented, creative women who, behind closed doors, are battling the uninvited guest who catches us unawares, pulling the rug from underneath us; quietly unravelling the capable versions of ourselves.

Production is stressful. There is no point pretending otherwise. Things change constantly. Clients change their minds, locations fall through, schedules move, budgets tighten, weather turns, equipment fails and somehow the work still has to get made.

There is an expectation to remain calm, pragmatic and reassuring, often at precisely the moment when everything around you feels uncertain. I am very aware that anxiety and production are not necessarily a natural fit, but this is the business I am in and it is also what I’m good at.

When I was 21, I had a severe panic attack and collapsed in public. It was like having an out of body experience: my body’s response was overwhelming, and completely out of my control. The spiralling fear and ‘noise’ in my head was crippling. Quite honestly, I thought I was dying. After the collapse I was unable to leave the house, I became agoraphobic for three months.

From that moment, my anxiety and I have walked side by side. It’s a constant in my life, like another family member popping in to say hello – mostly without warning, unwelcome and never at a good time – surprise surprise.

Six months after that first attack, I left home and went to London to start my first running job at SVC on Wardour Street. The anxiety and panic came along for the ride of course. I was just becoming an expert at masking them.

I am very aware that anxiety and production are not necessarily a natural fit, but this is the business I am in and it is also what I’m good at

You see, the person grappling with anxiety on the inside was not the same person London got to know and love in the mid 2000s. This woman was an energetic, vibrant and stylish young individual who stood out from the crowd and was often stopped to be photographed by the ‘streetstyle’ magazine photographers on Carnaby Street.

The external me was confident, daring even. But on the inside the battle raged on. There would be times on the number 19 bus into work where a panic attack was so bad I had to get off and find an alley to hide down for half an hour. An hour later, I’d turn up at work (now at M&C Saatchi), bringing the energy and vibrancy that was expected of me – or rather, that I expected of me.

Recently I wrote and produced a British short film titled Don’t See Me, which I developed with film director Lawrence Jacomelli. What is interesting to me now is that we did not set out to make a film about me. We set out to make a short film about a person living with anxiety because we wanted to bridge the gap before our next feature jumps into production.

The starting point was creative before it was confessional. That distinction matters, because it was only during the process, and perhaps even more when I looked back at what we had made, that I started to realise how much of myself was in it.

Sacha Parkinson plays Maddy, a young woman who has almost completely withdrawn from the outside world. She rarely leaves the house and has covered her windows with paper so that she cannot see out and nobody can see in. Maddy is not me and the events in the film are not a literal recreation of my life, but emotionally I recognised her more and more as the film developed.

That raised an uncomfortable question for me: if so much of the story was coming from my own experience, why did I not fully recognise that when we started? I think part of the answer is that I had spent so long separating anxiety from the rest of my identity that I had become used to thinking of it as something private, almost compartmentalised. I could talk about a character with anxiety much more easily than I could talk about myself.

Perhaps that is one of the strange things about making creative work. Sometimes you understand what you have made only after you have made it. Fiction gave me enough distance to approach something I might otherwise have continued avoiding. I had found a way to talk about anxiety through Maddy before I was ready to talk about it as Victoria.

That, for me, became the cathartic part of making the film. It was not simply the act of telling a story about anxiety. It was realising afterwards that I had been telling a story about something in myself that I had spent years keeping out of view. And that was both terrifying, and freeing at the same time.

Could I have written this article 15 years ago, around the time we were starting Beast Films? No. I do not think I was in a position to do it then. I would not have wanted colleagues, clients or people in the industry to know. Even now, I have moments when I question whether talking about it publicly is a good idea.

Getting your foot in the door as a young woman felt like a massive fucking privilege, and there was no way I was going to risk losing that bu showing my underbelly

I don’t want people to think, ‘ah, she’s not capable’. I started in advertising when it was still a very male dominated environment. And even though I worked with some incredible men, the feeling of imposter syndrome, or not being good enough, or the worry of dropping the ball at any point was massive.

Getting your foot in the door as a young woman felt like a massive fucking privilege, and there was no way I was going to risk losing that by showing my underbelly. What may have been perceived as ‘mental instability’. No way.

In fact, on the contrary. I can recognise now that my anxiety doubles up as my super power. I care deeply about the work I make. I care deeply about delivering work that a client loves. I work tirelessly on the adrenaline that my anxiety generates to make sure everything that my companies create is the absolute best it can be. I’m a hustler, a stickler, a perfectionist … and clients love that.

So what’s changed? Well, the way we talk about mental health. There is more openness and more understanding than there was when I first experienced panic attacks, and certainly more than there was when I began my career. There is also a lot more understanding about the hormonal complexities of women, specifically in their 40s, that certainly ramps things up another few notches – throw a bit of perimenopause in the mix, and you’ve got yourself a perfect storm!

That does not mean we are where we need to be. There is still a tendency to recognise mental health difficulties only when they become visible or when somebody can no longer function in the way people expect them to. In fact, I can’t name one person that I know personally from my work life who admits to suffering with anxiety. And I know that doesn’t mean some don’t. We need to keep talking about it, inside and outside the work space.

If somebody reads this and recognises something of themselves in it, I hope it makes them feel a little less inclined to believe they have to hide it from everyone around them

Anxiety is part of my life, but it is certainly not the whole of it. I am a creative director and a mother of two. I run two businesses. I also recently wrote and produced my first independent feature film, Blood Star, a desert thriller that we self-financed and shot in just ten days, now available on Prime Video and Apple TV. This spring, I’m preparing to produce my next feature film in Canada. And I also live with anxiety.

If somebody reads this and recognises something of themselves in it, I hope it makes them feel a little less inclined to believe they have to hide it from everyone around them. Anxiety does not make you less capable, less creative or less professional. On the contrary, it can allow us to feel deeply, notice the smallest details and anticipate what might happen next. All of these things are valuable when working successfully in production.

Of course, anxiety can be crippling. It can steal our confidence and leave us feeling out of control. But perhaps the power lies in trying to understand and accept it, rather than simply trying to control it. In doing so, we can perhaps prevent it from controlling us. This certainly helped me.

And lastly, balance. Those who know me well know I am horrific at finding time for myself and maintaining a work-life balance. When it is finally forced upon me, either through a good bollocking from someone close to me or a physical collapse from sheer exhaustion, I am reminded just how important that balance is, and how much of a difference it can make.

Anxiety doesn’t have to define us, and being able to manage it openly, without judgement, can make a huge difference. We need to keep the conversation open, both inside and outside the workplace. If being open about my own experience helps someone else, then talking about it has been worth it.

Victoria Taylor is creative director and co-founder at Beast Films; beast.agency

entry.title: Why SMLXL’s size is its strength
entry.summary: Creative Insight Why SMLXL’s size is its strength Being a team of just seven allows for the Barcelona and New York-based studio to be flexible and experimental in the projects it takes on, while also having fun By Laura Havlin 28/10/2026 3:27 am Creative industry awards specifica
entry.content:
Creative Insight

Why SMLXL’s size is its strength

Being a team of just seven allows for the Barcelona and New York-based studio to be flexible and experimental in the projects it takes on, while also having fun

By Laura Havlin 28/10/2026 3:27 am

Creative industry awards specifically designed to recognise the work of small agencies exist to give these outfits a fighting chance against the large agencies and global networks who have the budget and volume of work to flood entries into awards. A notable recent winner of one such prize is SMLXL, which picked up a Small Independent Design Agency of the Year gong at the D&AD Awards.

SMLXL was founded by Anna Berbiela, Guillem Casasús and Javier Arizu in 2024, but the trio, who met as students at EINA design school in Barcelona in 2008, had previously set up and run Pràctica with two other partners, a studio which they disbanded in 2024.

Coming back together was a risk – “it’s like getting back with your ex,” says Casasús – but what they learned from that experience they are putting into practice with SMLXL. This includes things like the optimum size, and more intangible factors such as creative fulfilment, and simply fun.

“If it doesn’t work out, at least let’s have fun,” says Arizu of the spirit in which they started again, though, as Berbiela adds, the aim was always to “make every project excellent” too.

entry.title: Smith & Diction create bold identity for Philadelphia Flower Show
entry.summary: Creative Inspiration Smith & Diction create bold identity for Philadelphia Flower Show For the 2027 edition, the design studio has stripped the identity back to its essentials, letting striking floral imagery and confident typography take the lead By Rebecca Fulleylove 28/10/2026
entry.content:
Creative Inspiration

Smith & Diction create bold identity for Philadelphia Flower Show

For the 2027 edition, the design studio has stripped the identity back to its essentials, letting striking floral imagery and confident typography take the lead

By Rebecca Fulleylove 28/10/2026 3:21 am

To celebrate the 200th anniversary of the Pennsylvania Horticultural Society (PHS), the 2027 Philadelphia Flower Show adopted the theme Iconic: a bold celebration of the garden and its cultural influence.

To create an identity to match, PHS enlisted Philadelphia-based design studio Smith & Diction. “This is one of those projects you accept immediately. The Philadelphia Flower Show is an incredible force here in Philly, so we were honored to be asked to be a small part of bringing it to life,” said co-founder Mike Smith.

With an early preview of the theme, the Flower Show team shared ideas centred on gardening as a source of “enduring beauty, sustenance and inspiration”. Smith and his team explored different ways to make flowers and gardens feel iconic, from texture and scale to colour and composition. “Ultimately one of our simplest ideas won out – the concept of photographing flowers in a way that makes them feel like monuments or fashion icons. Oversized. Stunningly lit. In perfect focus.”

The aim was to celebrate the beauty and diversity of nature, treating each bloom as a work of art. To complement the delicate floral imagery, the team introduced strong, simple design elements, balancing the organic forms of the flowers with a more structured visual identity.

Photography became the central focus, with lighting key to getting the balance right. “We wanted to hit exactly the right balance of dramatic, but not dark. We pulled a tonne of inspiration photos, and then we worked with Bre Furlong to capture the images, and honestly, she nailed it immediately.”

For the wordmark and typography, the studio chose Herbus by Ornamental Type, drawn to its bold elegance and references to late-20th-century typography. “With expressive geometry and striking silhouettes – it had the perfect vibe for this brand: beautiful, opinionated, and strong but with delicate moments and movement.”

The colour palette embraced drama, balancing a “deep, earthy moodiness” with moments of lightness. Gradients introduced additional colour and texture without competing with the flowers.

Finding the right blooms was another consideration. Keen to avoid the familiar selection of a standard florist, the team worked with New Jersey-based Main Wholesale Florist, which sourced special-order stems and opened up its warehouse for the designers to explore. “We got to walk through this fridge that’s legitimately the size of a house, and just wander and discover,” said Smith.

Once the flowers had been selected, the challenge was knowing what to leave out. With striking photography and expressive typography already doing the heavy lifting, the team found that restraint produced the strongest results.

“As a designer it can be oh so tempting to try and add your own fingerprints to the work, but in this particular case we had these incredible images and this incredible typography, and we found that using a super light touch with everything else felt best,” noted Smith. “We can’t tell you how many other designs we have on artboards that didn’t make it into the final brand materials, because in the end, keeping it simple ultimately won out.”

Rather than building an elaborate system of brand assets and application guidelines, the project became an exercise in getting the fundamentals right. “A well chosen subject. A beautifully lit photograph. An opinionated typeface. A clean and clear layout. It really can be that simple, if you get all the core elements exactly right,” added Smith.

“And ultimately, the brand isn’t meant to be super conceptual. There’s no hidden meaning or double read. It’s honestly just meant to feel kind of like wandering through a garden on a beautiful day.”

entry.title: Boomranng Studio creates charming branding for Cocoa & Katli
entry.summary: Creative Inspiration Boomranng Studio creates charming branding for Cocoa & Katli Offering sugar-free mithai and chocolates, the branding for the Indian sweet brand aims to emulate luxury, despite being health-conscious By Eliza Williams 27/10/2026 3:49 am Indian sweets tend to b
entry.content:
Creative Inspiration

Boomranng Studio creates charming branding for Cocoa & Katli

Offering sugar-free mithai and chocolates, the branding for the Indian sweet brand aims to emulate luxury, despite being health-conscious

By Eliza Williams 27/10/2026 3:49 am

Indian sweets tend to be associated with celebration and indulgence, but Cocoa & Katli wanted to create a contemporary style version of this that felt fresh and premium, “without slipping into the visual language of diet food”. The brand turned to Mumbai-based Boomranng Studio to help reposition it “as a bold, contemporary gourmet expression of Indian indulgence”.

“The name itself brings together two worlds,” says Boomranng. “Cocoa representing modern chocolate culture and Katli representing the familiarity and tradition of Indian mithai, giving the brand the best of both worlds. Instead of leaning into the traditional visual codes often associated with mithai, we created the Gourmet Forest, a surreal world where sweets and chocolates coexist.”

The resulting branding is colourful and expressive, designed to appeal to a younger generation rather than leaning into the nostagia often associated with traditional mithai. It features striking illustration that is nonetheless rooted in mithai heritage, however.

“The illustration language began by studying the familiar forms of Indian mithai, from the roundness of motichoor laddus, laddus, and pedhas to the sharp diamond geometry of kaju katli,” say Boomranng. “These recognisable shapes became the building blocks for a new visual world, reworked through sketches into characters, botanicals, ingredients, and surreal forms.

“To keep the system feeling contemporary, we paired these simple geometric and organic forms with soft gradients and subtle shadows, adding depth without making the illustrations overly rendered. The result is a playful, modern language that still feels rooted in the shapes and familiarity of Indian sweets.”

entry.content:
Creative Insight

Why Codea design studio has launched a shoe range

Codea co-founder Alex Marti explains how the new shoe line, created in partnership with Aka-research and SeaLlab, is part of an experiment in whether designing and selling products could be the key to creative and financial freedom

By Alex Marti 27/10/2026 3:48 am

Independent creative studios are in a good position at the moment, with the best of them able to offer clients value and new ways of thinking while many networked agencies are struggling. But are these independents going far enough? Sometimes the biggest existential questions can produce the boldest ideas. If you’ll indulge me, questions like, ‘What if we didn’t have any clients?’

We’re lucky to have a roster of clients that we love working with and in delivering projects, we move between arts, sports and fashion, always looking for the sweet spot between lifestyle and cultural relevance. This has given our studio members a certain perspective and a honed set of skills so it makes sense to push those in a different direction, designing our own products and bringing them to market.

I’m proud to say that we’ve done that and have just launched a range of shoes under new brand od.A at London’s Dover Street Market. The exclusive takeover of the shoe space and launch was timed to coincide with art fair Frieze London and also the launch of our new London office. There are two styles available, the 001 and 002.

entry.title: Dennis Vanderbroeck on creating live events that move people
entry.summary: Creative Process Dennis Vanderbroeck on creating live events that move people From his theatrical staging of Rosalía’s Lux tour to the pared-back styling of Icelandic composer Ólafur Arnalds’ new show, Vanderbroeck has become the master of the live spectacle By Paul Weedon 27/10/
entry.content:
Creative Process

Dennis Vanderbroeck on creating live events that move people

From his theatrical staging of Rosalía’s Lux tour to the pared-back styling of Icelandic composer Ólafur Arnalds’ new show, Vanderbroeck has become the master of the live spectacle

By Paul Weedon 27/10/2026 3:37 am

Studio Dennis Vanderbroeck was founded in Rotterdam in 2015 and operates with a core team of just six people. Yet it has quietly become a design force to be reckoned with, designing Miu Miu runway sets in Paris, staging the ambitious international concert run of Rosalía’s Lux tour, or – as it is currently – working on a production of Chekhov’s The Seagull at Eindhoven’s Parktheater.

After completing his bachelor degree in Performance Art at the Toneelacademie in Maastricht and a masters in Fine Art at Central Saint Martins in London, Vanderbroeck worked as a senior designer at set design and production company Bureau Betak in New York and Paris before establishing SDV with a commitment to working exclusively within physical spaces.

“The idea was always to have a hybrid practice,” he muses. “Because my only contacts were in theatre, it’s kind of where I started to build this thing. By expanding, fashion came into the picture and the practice grew organically to what it is now. I’m still with the same super small team and it’s quite amazing where we end up now; where the opportunities that come to us all feel so right, but are also extremely schizophrenic, in a way, which I absolutely love.”

Vanderbroeck’s theatrical sensibilities are what led Rosalía to seek out SDV as collaborators. Working alongside the Spanish singer and her creative team, they developed high-concept staging and immersive spatial design for her Lux listening party and subsequent world tour.

entry.title: Royal Designers for Industry rebrands as it turns 90
entry.summary: Creative Inspiration Royal Designers for Industry rebrands as it turns 90 The Royal Designers for Industry has been given a bold new identity by two of its most prolific members, Margaret Calvert and Ian Cartlidge By Daniel Milroy Maher 26/10/2026 11:56 am Renowned British design
entry.content:
Creative Inspiration

Royal Designers for Industry rebrands as it turns 90

The Royal Designers for Industry has been given a bold new identity by two of its most prolific members, Margaret Calvert and Ian Cartlidge

By Daniel Milroy Maher 26/10/2026 11:56 am

Renowned British designer Margaret Calvert marked her 90th birthday this year by unveiling a new identity for the Royal Designers for Industry (RDI), which also recently celebrated its own 90th anniversary. Established by the Royal Society of Arts in 1936, the RDI is the UK’s highest accolade for designers.

With a growing diversity of designers who hold the prestigious RDI title (only 200 can at any one time), the faculty felt it was time to rebrand – and who better to ask than two of their own members, Margaret Calvert and Ian Cartlidge.

Keen for typography to take centre stage, Calvert and Cartlidge developed the identity as a flexible framework built on Calvert’s existing typeface New Rail Alphabet, which she created with designer Henrik Kubel in 2009. Working predominantly around Calvert’s kitchen table, the pair slowly honed the work, removing devices and playing with letter spacing to achieve a refined look.

“The simpler it is, the better,” says Calvert. “At one point I started playing with tricks, linking the letters together, and then thought: no, we don’t need that, because this has got to be a lasting identity. The words are so important here, but it is also important to recognise where it has come from. The past is still the springboard.”

The resulting identity is simple, strong and adaptable, with the words ‘Royal Designers’ split across separate lines and rendered in a large size, to ensure engagement. When shortened to RDI, the acronym sits within a cyan circle, ready to be used across social media, and for the Faculty’s programmes, RDInsights and RDI Sessions, the same typeface is used to create a cohesive feel. These are also accompanied by a 90th mark that features an overlapping ‘9’ and ‘0’ in the same shade of blue.

Along with typography, colour played a key role in the rebrand, with the darker shade of blue that was previously used being replaced by cyan. This, Cartlidge explains, is because of the colour’s contemporary connotations, which appeal to a younger demographic of designers and make the faculty more visible to students.

Commenting on the pair’s design decisions, Cartlidge says: “The faculty isn’t a corporate institution; it’s a collection of designers. A flexible typographic framework felt much more appropriate than another fixed logo. It gives us something we can turn up or down depending on the context, but importantly it also gives other designers the tools to work with it and evolve it in their own way.”

Indeed, the RDI’s future was always the priority during Calvert and Cartlidge’s work on the identity. Now noticeably brighter and bolder, it better reflects the growing number of disciplines featured in the RDI 200, as well as the faculty’s ongoing mission to “connect generations and support emerging designers”.

entry.title: Applied Mschf on bringing its creativity to brands
entry.summary: Creative Leadership Applied Mschf on bringing its creativity to brands Launched to meet growing demand for Mschf’s distinctive approach, the commercial venture is carving out its own place in the industry. CR speaks to CEO Gabriel Whaley about preserving the collective’s independ
entry.content:
Creative Leadership

Applied Mschf on bringing its creativity to brands

Launched to meet growing demand for Mschf’s distinctive approach, the commercial venture is carving out its own place in the industry. CR speaks to CEO Gabriel Whaley about preserving the collective’s independent spirit and what he’s learned about agency life

By Rebecca Fulleylove 26/10/2026 3:50 am

Brooklyn-based art collective Mschf has made a name for itself with work that people can’t ignore. Since emerging in 2016, the group has turned unexpected ideas into tangible objects and internet moments, from its cartoonishly oversized Big Red Boots to a microscopic handbag, artwork made from medical bills and a Birkin bag reworked into a Birkenstock sandal.

In August 2025, the collective launched Applied Mschf, a commercial creative venture designed to bring its distinctive approach to culture into brand projects. For co-founder and CEO Gabriel Whaley, the move was a response to growing demand from brands.

“Ever since we started becoming more well known, we’d built an identity around a certain type of work that enters the world as a real thing that people can interact with, generates headlines and gets a lot of attention,” Whaley tells CR. “We were just doing that for ourselves really. There wasn’t necessarily a grand master plan beyond just engaging in the purest act of creation as rapidly as possible.”

But as brands increasingly approached Mschf for collaborations, Whaley realised the collective’s existing operation wasn’t equipped to handle them at scale. It has worked with established names in the past, including Crocs, Fenty Beauty and most recently an art exhibition with Lexus, but these projects brought different demands.

“What we realised is that there was this skyrocketing demand for external brand partnerships, but internally, we didn’t have the machine to accommodate that,” he says. “We spent the first five years building a machine to crank out any type of object, experience, website, on a two-week calendar.”

After meeting Kate Franklin, now president of Applied Mschf, whose background includes Complex and Vayner, Whaley saw how they could make it work for them.

“If we were going to do this seriously, I wanted to make sure that we had the right team around it,” he says. “Otherwise you end up with the same sort of frustrating game of a brand trying to collaborate with an artist, which generally can be quite friction-filled.”

Applied Mschf now has around 15 people within a wider Mschf group of just under 40. The distinction is deliberate. “[It] creates a context and a division between Mschf, the artistic practice, and Applied Mschf,” Whaley explains.

“Mschf can continue to do bold things and also attract the best talent, and [Applied Mschf] enables us to do that with brands and give it the proper focus and dedication…. There’s no mismatch of prioritisation.”

The agency’s launch offered a glimpse into how that approach might translate. Its announcement reworked the word ‘Applied’ through mash-ups of recognisable logos, including Ikea, Coca-Cola, Disney, Lego and Barbie.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by MSCHF (@mschf)

Although the two practices have different priorities, Whaley says the underlying approach remains much the same. He has never worked at a traditional creative agency, just as he didn’t set up Mschf with a background in art, media or fashion.

Instead, both businesses have been built from first principles: figuring out the most effective way to develop ideas and work with the right partners.

It’s like going to the gym. Everyone works out together. You exercise your brain

That means drawing on infrastructure already established across the wider group, with shared resources spanning design, production, finance, legal and HR. It also means keeping the creative process active even when there’s no immediate brief to solve.

Every day from 11am to noon, the company holds a brainstorm open to everyone, regardless of their role or whether they’re working on a client project. “It’s like going to the gym,” Whaley says. “Everyone works out together. You exercise your brain.”

The routine helps the team generate ideas quickly while exploring different categories, subcultures and formats. It’s particularly useful for a business whose enquiries range from major technology companies and Fortune 500 brands to K-pop groups. “The common thread is that there is no common thread,” Whaley says. “We just never know what email is going to hit the inbox this week.”

New partners also expose the team to unfamiliar industries, from automotive to AI and consumer packaged goods. But while the briefs may vary, Whaley says the starting point for a good client relationship is straightforward.

“It’s easy to convolute the goals and the KPIs with folks trying to talk what they think is our language,” he says. “We actually built a whole organisation to speak theirs.”

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by APPLIED MSCHF (@appliedmschf)

He wants clients to explain their business, product, audience and objectives in plain terms. It’s then up to Applied Mschf to find an unexpected way of meeting those goals. “We’ll test you. You don’t need to test yourself,” he says. That means the work isn’t tied to traditional advertising formats.

For Cash App, Applied Mschf created Cash Apples, a pixel-art game inspired by early internet clicker games. Players shook virtual trees to harvest apples, with the chance to win real money paid directly through Cash App. The simple mechanic turned a familiar digital pastime into an interactive brand experience.

In May 2026, the agency also helped skincare brand The Ordinary take its promise of accessibility beyond the bathroom cabinet. The Ordinary Bus was a free shuttle connecting Domino Park in Williamsburg with Prospect Park, cutting out a subway journey that could take more than 50 minutes.

While the service was suspended by the City less than a week into its planned two-week run, the idea applied the brand’s straightforward approach to a different everyday problem in an unexpected way.

More recently, the team created a brand identity for Life, a space mission searching for signs of life beyond our solar system. Drawing on retro-futurist imagery, the identity translates the science behind the mission into a visual language that carries across the project.

We need to respect that this person on the other side is working with the brand, and has worked a certain type of way for their career. They have their specific goals

The examples demonstrate the range of formats the agency can work with, and that flexibility also extends to how ideas are presented to clients. Depending on the concept, the team might develop a deck, write an essay, share artist sketches or build a quick prototype.

“There’s sort of a level of empathy,” Whaley says. “We need to respect that this person on the other side is working with the brand, and has worked a certain type of way for their career. They have their specific goals, their specific vision, their specific sense of accountability.”

That emphasis on collaboration also shapes the agency’s structure. Account management and production responsibilities are combined, so people help build the work rather than simply manage the client relationship. Creative directors are expected to take an idea from its initial spark through production and distribution. “The creative director is almost like the creative CEO of an idea,” Whaley says.

The challenge is to protect an idea’s vision without treating the client as an obstacle. Whaley sees the relationship as a partnership built around a shared objective, established at the outset and reinforced throughout the process. “It’s not about us having this perfect North Star of an idea, and you as a brand stepping in line,” he says. “It was put together to apply what we know towards a shared North Star.”

Increasingly, that work begins before the big idea takes shape. While brands approach Applied MSCHF for attention-grabbing creative, Whaley says one of the more surprising developments has been the demand for strategy.

He sees this as an opportunity to help brands understand their position within a wider cultural context: where they sit, what shapes their relevance and how they might respond to a changing landscape. “Mschf has proved that we are obviously good at making the noise, but we understand the meta that we all exist in and that we all share,” he says.

Whaley describes the approach as “the Gonzo version” of strategy consulting, drawing on the group’s cultural perspective to help brands articulate their place in the world and develop ideas that respond to it.

For all its creative ambition, however, Applied Mschf isn’t being built around rapid growth. When Whaley describes his ideal future for the business, he’s sitting in the group’s Brooklyn warehouse, and he has a specific goal for the space. “I’m telling myself right now that I never want to outgrow it,” he says.

The roughly 4,000-square-foot warehouse represents the kind of organisation he wants to preserve: a group of people who enjoy working together and making things they believe in, rather than a sprawling operation with layers of management between an idea and its execution.

Mschf began with the ambition of bringing creative people together to make things they’d want to make even if they weren’t being paid for it. Whaley wants Applied Mschf to retain that spirit. “If it’s not fun, the work sucks,” he says. “My priority right now is more like immortality than growing really fast.”

entry.title: New Children in Need campaign focuses on vital project workers
entry.summary: Creative Inspiration New Children in Need campaign focuses on vital project workers This subtle new film from BBC Creative emphasises the complex work that Children in Need workers perform to help support young people By Eliza Williams 26/10/2026 3:35 am It’s easy to focus on the
entry.content:
Creative Inspiration

New Children in Need campaign focuses on vital project workers

This subtle new film from BBC Creative emphasises the complex work that Children in Need workers perform to help support young people

By Eliza Williams 26/10/2026 3:35 am

It’s easy to focus on the fundraising work that BBC Children in Need does each year, which has an emphasis on fun and entertainment, with schools and children around the country all getting involved with its charity endeavours.

Behind this though lies the hugely important work that the charity does for children and young people, which often involves careful and consistent work by project workers to gain the trust of those needing support.

It is this that Children in Need’s new campaign film focuses on. The film follows Kai (played by Ethan Darby), a teenager reluctant to let others in, and Ryan (Charlie Rix), a project worker determined to earn his trust. Told through both of their perspectives, it explores how meaningful relationships are built over time, and the lasting difference a trusted connection can make in a young person’s life.

Crucial to the film’s success are the stellar performances by Darby and Rix, who are able to subtly articulate the small moments that are central to building a trusting relationship that in turn helps young people to thrive and build confidence.

Released in the run up to the BBC’s annual Children in Need appeal show, which takes place in the UK on November 13, the film is directed by Biscuit Filmworks’ Phoebe Arnstein, who comments: “I loved the duality of the script and the challenge of entwining the different perspectives of a child and a support worker both working out this unique and complex relationship.

“The story of the support worker is often overlooked and after talking to professionals in the field about their own experiences, I felt it was important to portray a character who doesn’t have all the answers straight away. It was this very human, unpolished and eventually rewarding story that drew me in.”
